extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning discrete mathematics / mathematical proof (matching theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Lecture-note guidance and proofs about matchings in bipartite graphs: statement of Hall's marriage condition, multiple proof strategies (Berge/augmenting-path, original transversal construction), and a statement/approach for the Kőnig–Egerváry theorem using adjacency matrices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hall's condition (Marriage condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Condition: every subset of k boys collectively fancy at least k girls. Theorem: There exists a matching for all b in B if and only if the condition (*) holds for all subset of B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central necessary-and-sufficient criterion for existence of a perfect matching (or a matching that covers B). The notes state the necessity direction is straightforward (if k boys fancy fewer than k girls a matching can't cover them), and the sufficiency is proven by the provided arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contrapositive using Berge's theorem / augmenting paths
rubrics_metrics.description: Use contrapositive: suppose a matching that covers B does not exist; choose a maximum matching M and an unmatched u in B; let Z be vertices reachable from u, Y = Z ∩ B, X = Z ∩ G. By Berge's theorem there is no augmenting path inside Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key steps given: because no augmenting path exists, any path starting at u must end at some b_i in Y; Z contains an odd number of vertices and |X| = |Y| - 1 < |Y|, which violates Hall's condition. This demonstrates the contrapositive sufficiency proof technique: find an unmatched vertex, analyze reachable set, and use augmenting-path/Berge reasoning to derive a violation of the marriage condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of bipartite graph from a set system to show equivalence with transversals
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a collection S = {S1, S2, ..., Sm} of subsets of a finite set S, construct a bipartite graph with one part the elements t1, t2, ..., tn and the other part S1, S2, ..., Sm; connect tj to Si iff tj ∈ Si.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This construction shows the equivalence: a transversal (m distinct elements, one in each Si) exists iff the union of any k subsets contains at least k elements iff the corresponding bipartite graph satisfies Hall's condition iff there is a perfect matching. The notes map 'elements' to 'girls' and 'subsets' to 'boys' to make the correspondence explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and criterion for a transversal
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition: A transversal is a set of m distinct elements of S, one in each Si.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The criterion given: S has a transversal ⇔ the union of any k subsets S_{i1},...,S_{ik} contains at least k distinct elements. The equivalence is demonstrated via the bipartite-graph construction and matching interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kőnig–Egerváry theorem (max matching size equals min vertex cover size) for bipartite graphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem: Let G be a bipartite graph. Let α'(G) be the number of edges in a maximum matching in G. Then α'(G) is equal to τ(G) (the size of a minimum vertex cover of G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notes assert equality of maximum matching size and minimum vertex-cover size for bipartite graphs; this is presented as a key structural criterion relating matchings and covers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjacency-matrix viewpoint for matching and covering
rubrics_metrics.description: Let M be the m×n adjacency matrix of a bipartite graph G with parts of sizes m and n. α'(G) equals the maximum number of 1's in the matrix with no two in the same row or column (a permutation-style packing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline given: represent edges by 1's in A; the maximum number of 1's with no two in the same row or column corresponds to a matching. A covering number τ(G) is related via r+s = τ(G) and counting arguments that compare placements of 1's and row/column covers. The notes sketch using the matrix to prove α'(G) = τ(G) (Kőnig–Egerváry) by exhibiting s 1's with no shared rows/columns and comparing to r + s = τ(G).
